arc_intro:
FQ-171 — Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

Let's get one of these instances launched properly, not just theorized about. karthik-dev needs a one-off instance to run a data migration script — pull some records, transform them, write the output somewhere durable. Simple enough on paper, but I want it done right: correct storage choices, correct way to connect, and correctly cleaned up afterward. That last part is where most people get it wrong.

— Ravi
arc_outro:
Ravi Krishnan — FQ-171 update:

Glad you caught karthik-dev's launch plan before he ran with it — instance-store-only for anything with output he cared about would've been a bad surprise. And the DeleteOnTermination lesson after he actually terminated it — losing the root volume's config changes but keeping the separately-attached output volume — that's exactly the kind of default setting people don't know exists until it costs them something.

Next: let's go deeper on actually managing a running instance day to day — not just launching one and walking away.

— Ravi

tasks.question: At a high level, what's the fundamental difference between STOPPING an EC2 instance and TERMINATING it?
options: A) They're functionally identical — both are permanent and cannot be undone

B) Stopping is reversible — the instance can be started again later, and its EBS-backed storage persists (though instance store data is still lost). Terminating is permanent — the instance itself is destroyed and cannot be restarted, and depending on volume settings, some or all of its storage may be deleted too
C) Stopping deletes all data immediately, while terminating preserves everything indefinitely
D) The only difference is billing — stopped instances are billed at a discounted rate, otherwise they behave identically to running instances

tasks.scenario: Before karthik-dev proceeds, you review his planned launch configuration.
tasks.broken_config:
Planned launch config for the migration script instance:
├── AMI: a community AMI advertised as "fast-boot, instance-store optimized"
├── Instance type: m5.large
├── Root volume: instance store (comes with the chosen AMI, no EBS root volume)
├── Additional storage: none planned — output was going to be written directly to the root volume
└── Plan: launch, run script (~2 hours), review output on the instance, terminate when done
what_to_find: The chosen AMI uses instance store for its ROOT volume — this means ALL data on the instance, including any output written to the root filesystem, is ephemeral and tied to the specific underlying host
No additional persistent storage is planned at all — the migration output (the entire point of running this script) would be written to ephemeral storage with no durable copy anywhere

The plan to 'review output on the instance, then terminate' is especially risky combined with instance-store root storage — if anything goes wrong between finishing the script and finishing the review, or if the instance needs a restart, the output could be lost before anyone even gets to use it
tasks.correct_fix: Either choose an EBS-backed AMI instead (so the root volume persists through stop/restart, though still lost on termination unless configured otherwise), or — better for this use case — attach a separate EBS volume specifically for the output, and write the script's output there rather than to the root volume at all.

tasks.scenario: karthik-dev asks: 'If I use an EBS-backed AMI for the root volume instead of instance-store, do I still need that separate additional EBS volume for output, or is the root volume enough?'
tasks.question: How should you answer?
options: A) The root volume alone is sufficient — a separate volume is never necessary once you're using an EBS-backed AMI

B) A separate volume is still the safer choice, even with an EBS-backed root — because by default, a root volume is set to be DELETED automatically on termination, while separately-attached (non-root) volumes default to being KEPT on termination unless explicitly configured otherwise. Output that matters is safer on a volume that survives termination by default
C) It doesn't matter either way — termination behavior is identical for root and non-root volumes
D) EBS-backed root volumes can never be terminated along with the instance, regardless of settings

tasks.scenario: The migration script completes successfully. karthik-dev copies the output volume's data to S3, confirms it looks correct, and then terminates the instance — thinking this is the clean way to close everything out. A day later, he realizes he'd also manually edited a config file directly on the root volume during setup, meaning to reference it later.
tasks.error_shown:
$ aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids i-0c4d8e2f1a9b3c7d6
"Reservations": []
(instance no longer exists; root volume also no longer appears under Elastic Block Store > Volumes)
tasks.diagnosis: The instance's root volume had DeleteOnTermination set to its default value (true). Terminating the instance therefore automatically deleted the root volume along with it — including the manually-edited config file that lived only there, with no other copy anywhere. The separate, attached EBS volume where the actual script output was written was NOT deleted, because non-root attached volumes default to DeleteOnTermination=false — that data was already safely copied to S3 anyway.
tasks.fix: Going forward: anything on a root volume that needs to survive termination must either be copied elsewhere BEFORE terminating, or the root volume's DeleteOnTermination flag must be explicitly set to false at launch (or via a console/CLI setting change before terminating) if the volume itself needs to persist as a snapshot or standalone volume afterward.
tasks.explanation: This exact real-world gotcha — 'terminate doing clean way' — ninaikkardhu, but root volume default DELETE will happen. Important anything root in volume only if it was (backup without), terminate did permanent pochu. This in T6 we saw concept's real consequence.

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks for a general guideline: for different kinds of EC2 workloads, when should the team default to STOPPING an instance between uses versus TERMINATING it?
options: A) Always terminate — stopped instances are pointless since they still exist in some form

B) Stop instances that are reused repeatedly with meaningful local state or slow startup configuration (e.g. a dev/test box used daily, or an instance with a lengthy manual setup); terminate instances that are truly one-off or fully reproducible from a script/AMI/Infrastructure-as-Code, where nothing valuable would be lost by starting fresh next time
C) Always stop, never terminate — terminating is inherently more dangerous and should be avoided entirely
D) The choice should be based purely on cost — always pick whichever is cheaper regardless of workload characteristics

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks about the cost implications of leaving an instance STOPPED (rather than terminated) for extended periods, since a few engineers have been doing this 'just in case' after finishing one-off tasks. An m5.large's EBS root volume (80GB gp3) costs roughly ₹640/month regardless of whether the instance is running or stopped; compute charges (~₹5,600/month if running continuously) stop entirely while an instance is stopped.
tasks.question: What's the real cost of the 'stop it just in case' habit, if instances are left stopped indefinitely instead of being properly terminated (with output already saved elsewhere)?
tasks.solution: Stopping eliminates the ~₹5,600/month compute cost, but the ~₹640/month EBS storage cost continues indefinitely for as long as the instance stays stopped — for a genuinely one-off task where the output is already safely copied elsewhere, this is pure ongoing waste with no benefit. Across a team of engineers each leaving a few instances stopped 'just in case,' this can add up to a meaningful, entirely avoidable monthly cost. The right call for truly one-off, reproducible work is to terminate once output is verified safe — not stop indefinitely.
tasks.explanation: This real cost habit — 'just in case' stop doing free not, EBS storage cost continue will happen. Output already safely irundha, indefinite stop doing waste only, with no real benefit.
